Q: How to pass multiple condtions to a CodeIgniter where() call A:

Your Query:

Associative array method:

$conditions = array(  'category_ID' => $caid,
                      'sold_date >=' => $prev_year_start_month,
                      'sold_date <=' => $prev_year_end_month
                    );
$query = $this->db->select_sum('sold_price')
                  ->from('tbl_sales')
                  ->where($conditions);
                  ->group_by('category_ID')
                  ->get()
                  ->row()

Q: How can I convert mp3/wav/m4a to aac using only vanilla JavaScript? A:

You don't.

With the exception of raw PCM that's probably in your WAV file, codecs like MP3 and AAC are complicated. It's not trivial to do, and there is no reason to do it unless you're trying to learn how codecs work or something.

Q: I built a database. What should I do next? A:

The point of a thesis depends on who grades it. To some, the point is to prove that you can work scientifically. To others, it's to make a small contribution to science. I think the point is not to do something big, but something valuable. Everyone who does actual research (not me) will gladly tell you all about what they are doing, and what tasks they break off into undergrad theses. Most of that work is to test some hypothesis by actually attempting the experiment. Success and failure are both valuable.

Q: facetting a stratified KM curve in ggsurvfit A:

It seems the issue here is not the facetting, but rather the output data produced by survfit2.

Consider

survfit2(Surv(time, status) ~ sex + surg, data = df_colon) %>% broom::tidy()

(Note that I've added surg to your model call. )

This gives:

# A tibble: 863 × 9
     time n.risk n.event n.censor estimate std.error conf.high conf.low strata                                        
    <dbl>  <dbl>   <dbl>    <dbl>    <dbl>     <dbl>     <dbl>    <dbl> <chr>                                         
 1 0.0219    328       1        0    0.997   0.00305     1        0.991 "sex=Female, surg=Limited Time Since Surgery "
 2 0.0986    327       1        0    0.994   0.00432     1        0.986 "sex=Female, surg=Limited Time Since Surgery "
 3 0.104     326       1        0    0.991   0.00530     1        0.981 "sex=Female, surg=Limited Time Since Surgery "
 4 0.110     325       1        0    0.988   0.00614     1.000    0.976 "sex=Female, surg=Limited Time Since Surgery "
 5 0.153     324       0        1    0.988   0.00614     1.000    0.976 "sex=Female, surg=Limited Time Since Surgery "
 6 0.197     323       1        0    0.985   0.00687     0.998    0.972 "sex=Female, surg=Limited Time Since Surgery "
 7 0.211     322       1        0    0.982   0.00755     0.996    0.967 "sex=Female, surg=Limited Time Since Surgery "
 8 0.216     321       1        0    0.979   0.00816     0.994    0.963 "sex=Female, surg=Limited Time Since Surgery "
 9 0.219     320       1        0    0.976   0.00874     0.992    0.959 "sex=Female, surg=Limited Time Since Surgery "
10 0.233     319       2        0    0.969   0.00981     0.988    0.951 "sex=Female, surg=Limited Time Since Surgery "
# ℹ 853 more rows
# ℹ Use `print(n = ...)` to see more rows

survfit2 has created a strata column containing a (labelled) version of all categorical variables in the model.

So neither sex nor surg are columns in the data frame that ggsurvfit takes as input. I've not explored further, but I suspect this means that you will need to replicate what ggsurvfit does in your own code in order to get your desired result. It shouldn't be too difficult: the input dataset contains all you need to create the plot: you just need to wrangle the strata column into separate columns to give you what you need.

Edit

Here's a crude demonstration of how you might roll your own.

First, wrangle the output from survfit2 to something more suited to your needs:

plotData <- survfit2(Surv(time, status) ~ sex + surg, data = df_colon) %>% 
  broom::tidy() %>% 
  mutate(
    tmp = str_split(strata, ",")
  ) %>% 
  unnest_wider(tmp, simplify = TRUE, names_sep = "_") %>% 
  mutate(
    sex = trimws(str_replace(tmp_1, "sex=", "")),
    surg = trimws(str_replace(tmp_2, "surg=", ""))
  ) %>% 
  select(-tmp_1, -tmp_2, -strata)


plotData

giving

and then

plotData %>% 
  ggplot() +
    geom_step(aes(x = time, y = estimate, colour = sex)) +
    geom_ribbon(aes(x = time, ymin = conf.low, ymax = conf.high, fill = sex), alpha = 0.25) +
  facet_wrap(~surg, nrow = 1)

Q: Best way to go from JSON to bash variables A:

Thank you so much for this extra, in-depth, example.

POSIX-compatible/"pure sh" code is a bit above my pay grade and level of experience. I never had to do anything in pure POSIX-sh. I Just know that it lacks most (all?) of Bash built-ins and hence more portable. I don't know enough about what is missing and how barebones sh is used to make up for lack of bash tools. I will study your latest example and compare to Bash-styled one and if I have any questions I will get back to our discussion.

From a brief glance, you are parsing JSON differently since sh doesn't have maps/associative arrays. You then set the parsed variables as globals from inside the function via eval, so they can be used by the code outside the function.
